title: Pathways to global hydrogen production within planetary boundaries

paper_content.abstract:
Hydrogen is a key lever for decarbonising hard-to-electrify sectors. Mitigation scenarios project an essential role for
hydrogen in returning within the climate change planetary boundary. Yet, its planetary footprint remains unclear,
particularly when Earth system interactions are considered. Here, we quantify the planetary footprint of global
clean hydrogen production using a bottom-up system model coupled with an Earth system interaction model. From
2025 to 2050, even under the most favourable scenarios, global hydrogen production is likely unsustainable,
confirming previous findings. We further show that Earth system interactions amplify hydrogen’s planetary
footprint. While electrolytic and abated fossil production are complementary, bio-based production is an order of
magnitude more unsustainable, as opposed to current trends. Our results contrast with the current focus on “green
hydrogen” which does not inform on its sustainability. Achieving sustainable hydrogen production will require the
reconsideration of viable production pathways, starting with the decarbonisation of existing production capacity.
paper_content.introduction:
The planetary boundaries framework emerges from Earth system science1. It delimits a safe operating space (SOS)
for human activities across nine critical processes guiding the stability and resilience of the Earth system1,2.
Currently, seven of these boundaries have been transgressed1–3. Outside the SOS, there is an increasing risk of
exceeding Earth-system tipping points, possibly triggering irreversible cascading effects1,4. In this context, there is a
global consensus to limit global warming well below 1.5 degree Celsius (°C) relative to preindustrial levels5–7. This
requires a rapid transition towards a sustainable economy, in which clean hydrogen is regarded as a key
decarbonisation lever for hard-to-electrify sectors and industries7–9. Terminology of key concepts is provided in
Supplementary Note 1.

Hydrogen could provide decarbonisation options for hard-to -electrify industries such as steelmaking, chemicals,
fertilisers, e-fuel synthesis, and transportation8,10,11. Consequently, mitigation scenarios limiting global warming to
1.5°C require a manifold increase in global clean hydrogen production7,12–15. Clean hydrogen production refers to
electrolytic, abated fossil and bio-based pathways16–18. Given the broad range of future applications for hydrogen,
ensuring that it remains within its dedicated share of the SOS (hereafter referred to as environmental space only) is
crucial19.

Recent absolute environmental sustainability assessments (hereafter referred to as sustainability assessment only)
found hydrogen production pathways to be unsustainable, with several planetary boundary transgressions20–23 (see
Supplementary Note 2). However, these studies20–23 assessed these pathways independently. Global hydrogen
production is unlikely to be provided by a single route or process but rather by a collection of processes operating
in a production system. Therefore, quantifying its sustainability remains a significant gap.

Recent climate change literature24,25 implies that only climate change mitigation scenarios leading to 1.9 watt per
square metre (W m-2 ) nameplate effective radiative forcing by 2100 (thereafter referred to as mitigation scenarios
only), could enable human operation within the climate change boundary. These scenarios are complementary to
additional mitigation measures for biodiversity and ecosystems26. Climate change and biosphere integrity are core
Earth-system processes with significant influence on the stability of the Earth-system which characterised the
Holocene epoch since the last glaciation1,27,28. These scenarios contain the necessary production volumes to
achieve the climate target. Therefore, environmental space allocation based on mitigation scenarios is essential. Yet
no study has comprehensively used this important contextualisation for allocating an environmental space to
global hydrogen production.

Sustainability assessment studies quantify planetary footprints of anthropogenic systems, but overlook Earth
system interactions29,30. The Earth system is composed of biophysically interacting processes, with amplifying or
stabilising feedbacks27,31. These feedbacks can ultimately shrink the SOS27. Implementing this important aspect
could reveal the effective planetary footprint of anthropogenic systems1,2,27,31. However, this aspect remains largely
unexplored in sustainability assessment studies.

Here, we address these gaps by quantifying the effective planetary footprint of global clean hydrogen production.
To this end, we develop a bottom-up production system model based on thirteen hydrogen production pathways to
minimise its effective planetary footprint. We use a mitigation scenario ensemble (n=32) from the
Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change Sixth Assessment Report (thereafter referred to as the AR6
ensemble)7,32 to define future production volumes and assign an environmental space to clean hydrogen
production based on its future utility. An overview of the approach is illustrated in Fig. 1. Our results show that
global clean hydrogen production is likely unsustainable with several planetary boundary transgressions, amplified
by biophysical interactions. Our assessment reveals that bio-based hydrogen production can amplify the planetary
footprint owing to significant burden shifts. In contrast, electrolytic and abated-fossil pathways can remain within
most planetary boundaries provided concomitant carbon capture and sequestration.
paper_content.results:
An environmental space for global clean hydrogen production
Our AR6 ensemble (n=32) implies a brief transgression of the high-risk threshold and sustained emission reduction
by 2100. The ensemble shows CO₂ concentrations rising to 453 (437-474) parts per million (ppm) by 2045 before
falling to ~401 (396-425) ppm by 2100 (Fig. 2a). This trajectory is consistent with the long-term target but briefly
overshoots the high-risk boundary (450 ppm) owing to historical emissions inertia. In the longer term, the CO₂
concentration decreases towards the planetary boundary (350 ppm) until it is reached in ~2150. By contrast, 2.6 W
m⁻² (~2°C warming) trajectories remain above the high-risk threshold for decades and stabilise in the zone of
increasing risks for centuries post-2100. These projections imply a significant decarbonisation of sectors and
industries, in which clean hydrogen could play an important role.

Decarbonisation efforts imply a rapid increase in clean hydrogen production volumes. Production volumes need to
increase from 2.58 (0.001-8.7) million metric tonnes of hydrogen per year (MtH₂ yr⁻¹) in 2025, to ~225 (68-460)
MtH₂ yr⁻¹ by 2050 (Fig. 2b). Recent studies12,16,33 report that only 0.8-0.95 MtH₂ yr⁻¹ was produced from clean
sources in 2025. Our AR6 ensemble, therefore, shows a current implementation gap of 1.63-1.78 MtH₂ yr⁻¹.
Meeting these production volumes would imply a compound annual growth rate of 19.6 (53.3 – 17.2) % from 2025
to 2050. These projections align with recent findings12 but remain lower than projections from the International
Energy Agency (IEA)'s net-zero scenario13 (NZE) for two reasons. First, the IEA integrates historical fossil production,
while most AR67 scenarios focus on clean hydrogen production12. Second, the role of hydrogen scales with
mitigation ambition – NZE target by 2050, whereas our ensemble follows a 1.9 W m⁻² trajectory by 2100. This
difference also shows how the assessment focus could shape the role of hydrogen in future energy systems.

A shrinking environmental space requires eco-efficiency improvements. The environmental space for global
hydrogen production reflects both the declining emission intensities of the energy system and the rising share of
hydrogen within it (Fig. 2c). Accordingly, the space available in 2025 is 9.53(6.74–13.78) percent of the SOS per year
and per giga metric ton of hydrogen (%SOS yr⁻¹ Gt H₂⁻¹), but by 2050, falls to 1.6 (0.76-5.57) %SOS yr⁻¹ Gt H₂⁻¹. Over
the 2025–2050 period, the average allocation is 4.54(2.8-9.26) %SOS GtH₂⁻¹. This contraction implies that hydrogen
production can only be sustainable if the system’s eco-efficiency improves at the same pace as the environmental
space shrinks.

Key hydrogen production pathways
The future production mix largely relies on abated fossil and electrolytic pathways. Optimisation results show that
together with the steam reforming (SMR) of fossil methane with carbon capture and sequestration (CCS), all water
electrolysis production routes are involved in the future production mix (Fig. 3b). In 2025, our results show that
24% (1.1 MtH2) needs to be produced from proton exchange membrane electrolysis (PEM), while alkaline
electrolysis (AE) provides 23% (~1.1 MtH2). Solid oxide electrolysis provides a relatively small share of the total
production (3% for 0.13 MtH2). The total contribution from water electrolysis is 49% (2.3 MtH2) of the total
production of hydrogen, while SMR-CCS provides 31% (1.44 MtH2), and SMR of biomethane with CCS is 20% (0.92
MtH2). For comparison, the IEA clean hydrogen projects database33 shows a higher reliance on water electrolysis
(54%) and SMR-CCS (43%). By 2050, the optimal production system relies on 63% (145 MtH2) of the total
production from water electrolysis, while the remaining 37% (84 MtH2) is provided by SMR-CCS. These results
indicate the strong reliance on both electrolysis and SMR-CCS, while bio-based production acts as a complement
when both the electrolytic and SMR-CCS pathways reach full capacity – consistent with recent projections14,16,18.

Water electrolysis implies a rapidly growing demand for low-emission electricity. Hydrogen production volumes
require a power mix dominated by wind, solar and hydropower, complemented by other low-emission alternatives
(Fig. 3d). In 2025, the system requires 0.1 petawatt-hour per year (PWh yr⁻¹) low-emission electricity. By 2050, total
electricity demand reaches 7.44 PWh yr⁻¹, equivalent to 83.3% of the current (202334) global production capacity.
This translates to 1.65 PWh yr⁻¹ (22%) and 4 PWh yr⁻¹ (54%) supplied by wind and solar energies alone. The power
mix also requires 1.17 PWh yr⁻¹ (16%) and 0.6 PWh yr⁻¹ (8%) from hydro and geothermal, respectively. This future
demand for renewable electricity is critical to minimise the planetary footprint. Without it, the optimal solution
shifts toward alternative routes, including bio-based production, thereby increasing pressure on the climate change
and biosphere integrity Earth system processes.

Planetary footprint of global clean hydrogen production
Without Earth system interactions, global hydrogen production is unsustainable across most boundaries. If
implemented, the production system would transgress six of nine planetary boundaries already in 2025 (Fig. 3a).
The production mix would transgress ~14 (10.5 - 21.5) times its dedicated environmental space for climate change
in 2025 and up to ~34 (11.9-93.7) times by 2050. Despite the low-emission nature of the system, transgressions
increase across all boundaries. For instance, we find a slight transgression representing 1.1 (0.82-1.56) times the
environmental space for biosphere integrity in 2025, while in 2050, this value increases to 4.2 (2.1-8.11). A more
significant evolution of the transgression is observed for the phosphorus biochemical flow boundaries, where the
impact dramatically increases from 23 (17-30.5) times in 2025 to 52 (31-164.6) times in 2050. The transgression
pattern reflects the mismatch between the shrinking environmental space (Fig. 2c) and the environmental
intensities of several processes (Fig. 4). More broadly, this illustrates the eco-efficiency mismatch between
prospective life cycle assessments (LCAs) and those assumed in mitigation scenarios.

Freshwater use remains within sustainable limits. In 2050, the optimal hydrogen production system requires ~9.2
cubic kilometre (km³) of blue water (41.4 km³ GtH₂⁻¹), consistent with previous estimates9,35 of 43.2 km³ GtH₂⁻¹ and
the 35.7–53 km³ GtH₂⁻¹ range36. Most of this demand (~45%) is embodied by solar power, primarily during silicon
manufacturing, cooling and purification (Fig. 4a). Water consumed directly in electrolysis accounts for ~25%,
reflecting both the reaction stoichiometry and cooling requirements. However, cooling water demand can be
substantially higher depending on meteorological conditions and water quality37,38, underlining that these global
results are likely an underestimation.

Land-system change is also within sustainable limits. At scale, the system requires ~58 square kilometre (km²),
equivalent to 1.43 × 10⁻4 % of global forested land39. Most of this impact (82%) arises from the construction of
natural gas pipelines for the SMR–CCS process (Fig. 4a). However, these values are likely underestimated.
Background inventories for wind and solar assume transformation of pastureland only, thereby excluding prior
conversion of forested land to pasture, as well as natural reforestation of pastures29. These omissions limit the
accuracy of current land-system change characterisation29.

Electricity supply and SMR-CCS are the dominant environmental hotspots. For climate change and ocean
acidification, embodied impacts of the renewable electricity mix account for ~40% of transgressions (Fig. 4a). Most
originate from manufacturing, where non-renewable energy is required at several stages; despite technological
improvements by 2050, embodied emissions remain non-negligible at scale. Solar thermal, although contributing
little to the overall supply, accounts for ~17% of these impacts, mainly due to industrial heat demand. Wind and
solar PV dominate pressures on biogeochemical flows, with nitrogen and phosphorus emissions linked to copper
mining and processing, including the use of explosives and sulfidic tailings. Direct emissions from SMR-CCS
contribute to ~32% of climate- and ocean-related transgressions, arising from carbon oxidation in reforming, the
water–gas shift reaction, and fuel combustion in the reformer furnace40. Even with CCS, SMR emits ~2.6 kilogram
CO₂ (kgCO₂) per kilogram of hydrogen (kgH₂⁻¹) in addition to embodied burdens. The natural gas feedstock account
for ~15% the total impacts, as both fossil extraction and biogas upgrading release significant carbon emissions.
Overall, renewable electricity and SMR–CCS together drive ~78% of the footprint across boundaries, except for
stratospheric ozone depletion, where end-of-life treatment and transport of scrap steel from alkaline electrolyser
recycling accounts for ~41% of impacts.

With Earth system biophysical interactions, the planetary footprint is strongly amplified. These interactions (via
feedback loops) can either stabilise or amplify pressures. In 2025, the amplification drives previously negligible
impacts on freshwater and land-system change to transgressions of 5.5 times (4.3–6.6) and 11 times (8.6–13.2)
their boundaries, respectively (Fig. 3c). Core boundaries are affected even more. Climate change transgressions
rise by 83%, and biosphere integrity increases by 1511%. Amplification increases towards 2050, owing to the
contraction of environmental space, and results in a more even distribution of pressures (equilibrium) across Earth-
system processes (Fig. 3b) – revealing the effective system-wide footprint of individual processes (Fig. 4b).

This equilibrium has critical implications. Alleviating pressures on one boundary, such as climate change, at the
expense of another, yields limited benefits because of feedback loops propagating impacts across the Earth-system,
e.g., bio-based production30,41,42(Fig. 4b). Thus, capturing the effective planetary footprint requires sustainability
assessments to include biophysical interactions.

Sustainability of alternative hydrogen production systems
Electrolytic hydrogen production shows the lowest planetary footprint. The electrolytic system is composed of
proton exchange membrane (~60%), alkaline (~29%), and solid oxide (~10%) electrolysis technologies in 2050
(Supplementary Fig.18). This system would require ~12 PWh of electricity, exceeding today’s renewable output of
~8.9 PWh and approaching half of the solar and wind generation projected by the IEA18 for 2035 (18.2–23.2 PWh).
Despite the consequent renewable electricity demand, this system transgresses 5 out of 9 planetary boundaries
(Fig. 5a). For instance, the impact on climate change exceeds the environmental space ~12 times while ocean
acidification is exceeded ~4 times. Biosphere integrity boundary is also exceeded ~2 times. These transgressions
originate from embodied emissions of renewable electricity generation technologies. With biophysical interactions
(Fig. 5b), the climate change and biosphere integrity boundaries are transgressed ~41 and ~26 times. In comparison
to abated fossil and bio-based production, electrolytic production continues to show the lowest planetary
footprint, making it the closest pathway to sustainability, provided a matched deployment of renewable electricity
capacity.

Abated-fossil production performs similarly to electrolysis. In 2050, the fossil-based system consists primarily of
SMR-CCS (~96%) and coal gasification with CCS (~4%) (Supplementary Fig.22). This system transgresses five
planetary boundaries in 2050. Climate change is transgressed ~41 times, and ocean acidification ~14 times, owing
to the remaining direct CO₂ emissions from reforming reactions and combustion in reformer furnaces in the SMR
process. Additional transgressions occur in phosphorus biochemical flows (transgressed by ~40 times), and
biosphere integrity (exceeded by ~3 times). While CCS reduces pressures compared with unabated fossil
production, the system remains unsustainable in absolute terms. With biophysical interactions (Fig. 5b), the
planetary footprint of abated-fossil is in the same order of magnitude of the electrolytic production system –
climate change and biosphere integrity transgressed ~58 times and ~42 times, respectively. Given the current clean
hydrogen implementation gap43, these results imply that retrofitting existing fossil capacity with CCS18 to
complement electrolysis could be meaningful. However, this requires sufficient CO₂ storage capacity44 and ensuring
that potential CCS lock-in45,46 does not hinder the complete phase out of fossil fuel (Discussion).

Bio-based hydrogen production amplifies planetary boundary transgressions. At scale, the biomass-based system
includes steam biomethane reforming with (~30%) and without (~67%) CCS as well as the gasification of (poplar)
woodchips with CCS (3%) (Supplementary Fig.20). Under this configuration, the system transgresses six planetary
boundaries, with particularly high impact on climate change (exceeded ~174 times) and biosphere integrity
(exceeded ~16 times) (Fig. 5a). These impacts reflect on the use of wood chips (~80%) of biosphere integrity
impact, and emissions from biomethane upgrading, reforming and water-gas shift reactions (~98% climate change
and ocean acidification impact). With biophysical interactions, the footprint is further amplified (Fig. 5b). Unlike
electrolysis and fossil-CCS systems, bio-based production shows the worst planetary footprint – climate change and
biosphere integrity transgressed ~229 and 180 times – consistent with its exclusion from the reference production
system (Fig. 3b). Further information in these alternative production systems is provided in Supplementary Note
10.

Direct air capture and sequestration to mitigate the planetary footprint
Direct air capture and sequestration (DACS) can mitigate most boundary transgressions. With biophysical
interactions, DACS provides a mechanism to stabilise the effective planetary footprint of hydrogen production by
mitigating climate change. Optimisation results show that DACS has the potential to reduce transgressions in nearly
all categories (Fig. 6). In 2025, a 5.31 kgCO₂ kgH₂-1 DACS rate is required, while in 2050, it decreases to 3.86 kgCO₂
kgH₂-1 (Fig. 6a-b, d and g-i). On average, ~4.13 kgCO₂ kgH₂-1 yr-1 must be captured between 2025 and 2050 to
maintain hydrogen production within its allocated environmental space. At scale, this represents 0.93 giga metric
ton of CO2 per year (GtCO2 yr-1). DACS, however, is unable to offset pressures on biochemical flows owing to the
system’s reliance on renewable electricity. The significant nitrogen and phosphorus emissions that occur during
copper mining, for both wind and solar power infrastructure, outweigh DACS benefits for these Earth system
processes (Fig. 6e and f).

Concurrent DACS can increase the system’s electricity requirement significantly. Optimisation consistently favours
heat pump-based DACS systems powered by renewable energy. Generally, after CO2 capture, heat is required in
DAC systems to release CO2 from the binding sorbent or solvent47. In 2050, the DACS energy consumption is 0.95
kilowatt hour (kWh) per kgCO2. Reaching sustainability in most boundaries at scale (i.e., 225MtH2 yr-1) would
require an additional 2.2PWh of electricity (9.75PWh total) for capturing and sequestrating CO2. This estimation is
relatively high but remains lower than the 12TWh for hydrogen production estimated in the IEA NZE scenario18.
The required DACS rate could vary strongly depending on the system configuration. The electrolysis-based system
requires ~4 kgCO₂ kgH₂-1 yr-1 (Supplementary Fig. 24), compared with ~5.3 kgCO₂ kgH₂-1 yr-1 for a fossil with CCS-
based system and ~17 kgCO₂ kgH₂-1 yr-1 for a bio-based system (Supplementary Fig. 25 and Supplementary Fig. 26).
These DACS rates reflect the underlying emission drivers. For the electrolytic system, the DACS rate would primarily
offset the embodied impacts of renewable energy, while for the fossil with CCS system, the remaining direct
emissions of carbon dioxide would be mitigated. The relatively high DACS rate for bio-based production can be
explained by the emission intensities of processes involved, as well as the impact on biosphere integrity. These
DACS rates would require 14.23PWh, 2.58PWh, and 3.84PWh of total renewable electricity for the electrolytic,
abated fossil and bio-based systems, respectively. Compared to the 12PWh projected in the IEA NZE scenario, these
results highlight that achieving sustainability for hydrogen cannot rely on water electrolysis alone unless a massive
increase in renewable electricity capacity is deployed concomitantly.

Hydrogen leakages can reduce the benefits of carbon capture and sequestration. Hydrogen is a difficult gas to
manage, and leakages could be significant12,48,49. At an optimal DACS rate (i. e., 3.86 kgCO₂ kgH₂⁻¹ in 2050), if 10% of
production is leaked, the impact on climate change could increase by ~480% (Supplementary Fig.27). To offset
these leakages, an additional 0.63 kgCO₂ kgH₂⁻¹ would be necessary (Supplementary Note 11), thereby increasing
the system electricity requirement. At scale (i.e., ~225MtH2), this represents an additional 0.142GtCO2 captured
and sequestrated, requiring 0.135PWh of renewable electricity. Given potential constraints in both DACS and
renewable energy capacity18,44, achieving sustainability for hydrogen will also depend on controlling potential H₂
leakages.
paper_content.methods:
Goal and scope of the study
This study aims to quantify the effective planetary footprint of global hydrogen production and identify key
production pathways. More specifically, we focus on future clean hydrogen production volumes expected to
replace the current fossil-based production capacity16. To this end, we conduct an absolute environmental
sustainability assessment aligned with recommendations from Bjørn et al.87 and based on an attributional cradle-
to-gate prospective LCA. We define the functional unit as the “global annual hydrogen production with optional
direct air capture and sequestration of carbon dioxide” with no further specifications on the thermodynamic state
or quality. The temporal scope spans from 2025 to 2050 with a 5-year time step, as the hydrogen economy is
expected to grow sharply in that time frame45.

Future hydrogen production volumes are consistent with a 1.9-2.25 W m-2 target by 2100. We obtained these
projections from a scenario ensemble (n=32) derived from the AR67,32. From the same ensemble, we further
derived a utilitarian-based downscaling approach to allocate an environmental space to global hydrogen
production. Such an approach defines an environmental space and quantifies hydrogen production volumes. This
robust approach is also in line with some of the recent recommendations from de Bortoli et al.78.

Thirteen hydrogen production processes were considered for building the life cycle inventory. These include key
electrolytic-, abated-fossil-, and bio-based pathways (Supplementary Table 6). Background data are sourced from
the Ecoinvent 3.9.1 "cut-off by classification" database. Following the approach of Bachmann et al.30, whenever
possible, the selected data focuses on the "World" and "GLO" locations. When background inventories are
unavailable at these locations, conservative locations were selected, such as Europe "EUR" and "Europe without
Switzerland". Alternatively, for the same reason, the rest of the world (ROW) location is chosen as a proxy. When
data was unavailable at these locations, Germany (DE) was chosen. This is because Germany is likely to become one
of the largest hydrogen producers in Europe9,54,89. Here, it is worth noting that this approach introduces
uncertainties, as the processes involved may not accurately reflect global averages.

We obtain prospective LCA matrices using the premise software v2.2.679 and aggregated all meaningful inventories
to decrease computation times. In a subsequent step, we reduced the number of matrices by creating sampling
matrices using Triangular distributions with the Julia package Distributions.jl90. More specifically, we opted for
triangular distributions to remain within the bounds of the selected scenarios. The matrices obtained would
contain the minimums, maximums, and modes, thereby reducing the number of matrices that need to be
manipulated. The modes were defined as the median of values across scenarios. The approach is further described
in Supplementary Note 7. However, we do not account for uncertainties in the background system following the
conclusions from Marsh et al.83. Similarly, we do not account for uncertainties in the foreground system, as process
parameters could not be retrieved along with matrices. We also do not account for uncertainties from
characterisation, as we could not obtain uncertainty parameters from previous work29,30,85. Thus, the uncertainty
range reflects values across selected mitigation scenarios only.

We used a linear programming (LP) model to minimise the effective planetary footprint of global hydrogen
production. The LP model selects and identifies the optimal scale of technology options to minimise transgression
across planetary boundaries, considering biophysical interactions. The model is built using the Julia programming
language91 v1.10, JuMP.jl92 v1.27.0, and CPLEX as the optimisation solver. Modelling constraints were directly
sourced from the scenario ensemble derived from the AR67,32.

Mitigation scenarios ensemble definition
As previously mentioned, we derived a scenario ensemble (n=32) from the AR67,32 consistent with 1.9-2.25 W m-2
total radiative forcing by 2100. To ensure consistency, we computed future radiative forcing values using the FaIR93
v2.2.1 base model – replicating the AR66 results. These were compared with the radiative forcing concentration for
atmospheric CO2 reported values from the AR66.

Next, we screened mitigation scenarios in the AR6 dataset32. We selected the “AR6 climate diagnostics|Effective
Radiative Forcing|FaIRv1.6.2|50.0th Percentile” ( W m-2) variable and imposed a maximum of 2.25 W m-2 (average
between 1.9 and 2.6 W m-2) variable in 2100. From the AR66, the 1.9 W m-2 by 2100 target represents a nameplate
category of scenarios6. From each scenario, we extracted the "Emissions|CO2" variable (MtCO2 yr-1) for each year.
Because these scenarios do not provide the forcing and concentration of CO2, these had to be computed for the
ensemble validation.

For scenario ensemble validation, we modelled the integrated impulse response function of CO2 49 (Equation (1))
which we used to derive the concentration 𝐶𝑡 (Equation (2)) and radiative forcing 𝐹𝑡 (Equation (3)) for CO2. In these
equations, 𝑘𝑡 the cumulative decay of CO2 for a year 𝑡 in the period 𝑇, 𝜏𝑖 and 𝛼𝑖 are the lifetime and decay
parameters, respectively. Further, 𝑞𝑎𝑖𝑟 is the air mixing ratio48, 𝑀𝐶𝑂2 the molar mass and 𝜀𝐶𝑂2 the effective radiative
forcing of CO2. Parameters for Equation (1) to Equation (3) are available in Supplementary Table 13. Lastly, for
validation, we compared the computed values from the ensemble with results from FaIR93 v2.2.1 modelling and the
AR6 projections6.

The AR6 ensemble is independent of the prospective LCA scenario ensemble we derived from premise Python
package v2.2.679. We computed radiative forcing and atmospheric concentration of CO2 trajectories for both
ensemble and compared them against a FaIR93 v2.2.1 model and the AR6 projections6 for validation. We found
four matching scenarios, namely REMIND SSP1- SSP2- and SSP5-, PkBudg500, as well as IMAGE SSP2-1.9. TIAM-UCL
SSP2-1.9 was available but excluded due to an important mismatch with a 1.9 W m-2 target by 2100. Ultimately, we
also excluded the IMAGE SSP2-1.9 scenario due to a dimension mismatch in the LCA matrices, which we were
unable to resolve.

To summarise, we derived the AR6 ensemble (n=32) consistent with a 1.9-2.25 W m-2 target by 2100, which
includes future hydrogen production volumes and technology constraints, such as the availability of wind and solar
electricity. Prospective LCA matrices were derived from a smaller ensemble (n=3) consisting of REMIND SSPx-
PkBudg500 scenarios. Both ensembles were validated against the 1.9-2.25 W m-2 target by 2100 (Supplementary
Note 9).

Hydrogen production pathways
Each production pathway was modelled as a cradle-to-gate process consistent with our system boundaries. More
details on the production pathways are available in Supplementary Note 3, and life cycle inventories are provided in
Supplementary Table 6.

Electrolysis technologies were included. Low-temperature technologies cover alkaline electrolysis (AE) and proton
exchange membrane (PEM) electrolysis, both operating at 60–80 °C55. AE is a mature and cost-effective technology,
while PEM systems offer higher efficiency and compact design but are constrained by the availability of iridium and
platinum catalysts55,56. Anion exchange membrane (AEM) electrolysis is an emerging option, but it was not
considered here due to its limited commercial maturity. High-temperature electrolysis was represented by solid
oxide electrolysis cells (SOEC), which operate at 700–1,000 °C using steam to reduce electricity demand. SOECs
achieve higher efficiencies but face material degradation challenges that limit their current commercial
deployment15,55.

Methane-based production pathways include steam methane reforming (SMR) and methane pyrolysis (MP). SMR
was included as it is the current dominant production route. The process uses nickel catalysts at 700–1,000 °C and
can be combined with carbon capture and storage (CCS)40. MP was also considered as a low-carbon alternative,
splitting methane into hydrogen and solid carbon. MP requires more methane input on a stoichiometric basis and
is technically challenging to implement, but it avoids carbon oxidation. For these processes, methane can be
sourced from fossil origins or from upgraded biogas.

Coal and biomass gasification production pathways were also considered. Coal gasification operates at
temperatures ranging from 800 to 1,300 °C and produces syngas, a mixture composed of H₂, CO, and CO₂45.
Biomass gasification uses feedstocks such as wood chips or residues and generates syngas alongside char and tar.
Both processes employ water-gas shift reactions and syngas purification to maximise hydrogen yield94. CCS can be
applied to reduce the emission intensity of both coal- and biomass-based hydrogen.

Electricity supply
The electricity generation mix reflects the scenario ensemble projections (Supplementary Fig. 14). The scenario
ensemble indicates a decline in coal and unabated gas, offset by rapid growth in wind and solar, and with more
moderate but sustained roles for hydro, nuclear and biomass. A complete list of the inventories used is provided in
the Supplementary Table 7.

We include renewables and nuclear sources as low-emission alternatives, consistent with long-term
decarbonisation trends. These include onshore wind turbines, solar photovoltaic and solar thermal plants, run-of-
river hydropower, geothermal power, and nuclear power from three reactor configurations: boiling water,
pressurised water, and heavy water-moderated pressurised reactors.

Carbon dioxide capture and sequestration
Carbon capture and storage technologies act as decarbonisation levers to achieve carbon neutrality before 205095.
CCS can be combined with several hydrogen production processes, such as SMR, biomethane steam reforming, and
coal and biomass gasification. For processes with significant carbon outputs, such as steam methane reforming and
coal gasification, CCS can be used at plant sites to capture CO2 directly from flue gas (CO2-rich exhaust gas)40.
Inventories we use from the premise software v2.2.6 already include CCS (e.g., SMR, biomass gasification with
CCS).

For additional carbon capture, we use the direct air capture and sequestration of carbon dioxide (DACS). We
consider large-scale (1 MtCO2) solvent-based systems with heat either supplied by a heat pump or industrial
steam47. Inventories for these processes are listed in the Supplementary Table 8.

Planetary boundary impact characterisation
We assess the direct impact of global hydrogen production on 8 out of the 9 Earth-system processes defined in the
planetary boundaries framework. These are climate change, ocean acidification, atmospheric aerosol loading,
freshwater use, biogeochemical flow (phosphorus and nitrogen), stratospheric ozone depletion, land-system
change and changes in biosphere integrity. All characterisation factors originate from Bachmann et al.30 initially
based on the work of Ryberg et al.29 and Galán-Martín et al85. In addition, we calculated a hydrogen
characterisation factor for climate change to evaluate the effect of potential leakages (Supplementary Note 8).

Although the recent progress on the definition of control variables for novel entities96 is encouraging, we do not
assess the impact on this Earth-system process since we could not define a boundary value29,96. Also, as previously
mentioned, we do not account for uncertainties of the characterisation method due to a lack of data. Additionally,
we exclude biogenic carbon accounting as there is likely a temporal mismatch between carbon uptake and emission
during hydrogen production.

Although crucially important, the environmental response (including feedback loops in the Earth system) was not
modelled in previous characterisation methods29,30,85 owing to the inherent complexity. In this work, we extend
previous methods by integrating the interaction model from Lade et al.27. This simple model, while at an infancy
stage of development27, would account for amplifying or stabilising feedbacks between different Earth-system
processes. Ultimately, this would lead to a certain impact equilibrium that is not captured in conventional
sustainability assessments (Supplementary Note 6).

receiving biophysical system 𝑘 and 𝐈∈ℝ𝑧×𝑘 the identity matrix. 𝐁 was sourced from Lade et al.27. The formulation
in Equation (4), in the form of the Leontief matrix, would account for feedback loops between Earth system

To be sustainable, global hydrogen production must remain within its dedicated environmental space. To define
this space, we allocate a share of the global SOS to global hydrogen production using a utilitarian downscaling

reviewer_comments.reviewer_1:
The manuscript presents a modeling-based assessment of global hydrogen production and its sustainability within planetary boundaries. While the topic is relevant, the study in its current form raises concerns that prevent it from being suitable for publication in Nature Communications. The paper relies entirely on a modeling approach that remains unclear in its hypotheses, methodological choices, and model specifics, leading to surprising and unexplained results. For instance, the authors find that hydrogen production worsens ocean acidification, yet it is unclear whether this is simply a consequence of fossil fuel use or whether other mechanisms are at play. At the same time, they suggest that hydrogen reduces pressure on freshwater resources, which contradicts existing literature indicating hydrogen’s high water footprint compared to other energy sources (Olaitan et al., 2024, STOTEN). With such a simulation-based experiment, it is difficult to determine whether these outcomes reflect real-world mechanisms or are merely artifacts of model assumptions. The model appears to function as a black box, with results being presented quantitatively but without sufficient critical interpretation.
The manuscript also overlooks key physical processes that could significantly alter its conclusions. Notably, hydrogen is an indirect greenhouse gas, yet this effect is neither referenced nor incorporated into the model, raising concerns about the completeness of the analysis. Additionally, the choice of a 1.5°C scenario is questionable, as this target is increasingly viewed as unattainable. The rationale for focusing on this specific pathway is not clearly articulated, nor is its relevance to the broader discussion of planetary boundaries and hydrogen sustainability.
While planetary boundaries provide a useful rhetorical framework for discussing environmental sustainability, they remain more of a conceptual tool than a precise scientific paradigm. This distinction should be made clearer in the text.
Beyond these scientific concerns, the manuscript is difficult to follow due to its dense structure and convoluted explanations. Methodological details are scattered throughout the text, making it challenging for the reader to assess the rigor of the approach. The conclusions, while ambitious, remain highly speculative given the limitations of the study. Without a clearer justification of assumptions, a more transparent discussion of uncertainties, and some degree of empirical validation, the paper does not meet the publication standards of Nature Communications.
reviewer_comments.reviewer_2:
The authors provide a comprehensive analysis of the environmental impacts of future global hydrogen production using a planetary boundary-based prospective LCA framework combined with mathematical optimization. I found the article interesting and believe it has the potential to make a contribution to both the LCA and hydrogen literature. However, a key concern is that the methodology is difficult to follow. I outline my specific comments below.
1. The methodological approach is quite difficult to follow. First, it is unclear how your bottom-up hydrogen production system model integrates with the annual hydrogen demand in the SSP1-PkBudg500 scenario. If REMIND already considers hydrogen, then its scenario results include a specific technology mix that meets this demand while satisfying the climate target and other constraints within the model. If I understood it correctly, your model determine a new optimal mix that minimizes the planetary footprint (or only for the electricity mix that supplies electrolytic hydrogen production?). If so, I was wondering to what extent is this consistent? Will the new optimal mix ensure that the interactions between the hydrogen sector and other sectors in the IAM scenario remain coherent? For example, in the SI it is stated that “allows the model to go beyond the capacity initially defined by the SSP”. For instance, could your optimized hydrogen production mix lead to excessively high system costs, potentially affecting the results of the IAM model?
2. By focusing on the global scale, the authors rely on LCIs that reflect global, European, RoW, or German averages. This introduces significant uncertainty, particularly for electrolytic hydrogen powered by renewable energy, given the large variability in capacity factors. As shown in studies such as Wei et al. or de Kleijne et al. (works that the authors cite), the carbon footprint (and potentially other impacts) of hydrogen production can vary widely even across major regions. Similarly, the impacts of various power generation technologies like coal, natural gas, or hydro can vary widely depending on the location. While the authors acknowledge this limitation (page 17, line 543) and note that these uncertainties are not addressed in this work, I believe this issue has major implications and warrants further discussion. For instance, to what extent do the average datasets used in this study accurately represent a truly global average process?
3. The implementation of interactions between planetary boundaries is not entirely clear. At page 7, line 225, the authors provide the following example of biophysically mediated interactions: “clearing land leads to carbon dioxide emission to the atmosphere. Thus, a significant change in the LSC control variable would influence the boundary for CC.” This raises the question of whether these additional CO2 emissions from land clearing should be accounted for in the life cycle inventory, thereby directly contributing to the quantification of the CC planetary boundary. If these emissions are captured within the LCI, what is the added value of explicitly modeling these interactions? I suggest that the authors further clarify their rationale and provide a more detailed explanation of how these interactions are integrated into their approach.
4. The readability of the Results section could be improved. Presenting the planetary footprint right away, without first describing the optimal hydrogen production mix, provides little context for understanding the results. I suggest first introducing the hydrogen mix that minimizes the planetary footprint (i.e., the current Figure 3) before discussing its planetary footprint (current Figure 2).
5. A key takeaway from the study is that “using biomass-based sources for hydrogen production will significantly impact the biosphere integrity boundary. This result directly contradicts hydrogen applications relying on biomass”. However, if I understand correctly, wood chip is the only biomass feedstock considered for the gasification route. This overlooks other biomass residues that do not compete for land (e.g., with food) and/or have lower or no land requirements. Could the authors further elaborate on how their choice of biomass feedstock influences this conclusion?
6. On page 16, line 503, the authors suggest that "it is better to focus on a certification scheme informing the planetary footprint of hydrogen (impact on all planetary boundaries)". While this sounds like a great idea, simply mentioning it does not add much depth. I wonder, for example, to what extent such an approach is practically feasible. I believe the authors should elaborate further on how they envision the implementation of such a certification scheme.
7. On page 17, line 521, the authors suggest that their approach could help strengthen the integration between LCA and IAM. While this has been a long-standing topic in the literature, practical progress has been limited. Other studies have already developed optimization models on top of IAM scenarios (e.g., the PULPO framework cited by the authors). Therefore, it remains unclear how their approach advances this integration. Similar to the certification scheme, the authors should provide further clarification on their specific contribution.
8. I believe the authors could better emphasize the novel findings in the abstract. For instance, on page 9, line 275, they state: “The addition of interaction parameters to evaluate the absolute sustainability of hydrogen shows a strong amplification of impact.” This appears to be a key novel finding of the study, yet it is not mentioned in the abstract.
Other minor comments:
- Page 3, line 125, please note that the hydrogen production scenarios assessed in Wei et al. are based on IEA scenarios.
- At several places across the manuscript, there is a mix between carbon dioxide removal (CDR, removal of CO2 from the atmosphere) and carbon capture and storage. For example, at page 6 line 201, biomass with carbon capture and storage would be a more appropriate term than “biomass with a carbon removal”.
- Page 9, line 287: I don’t believe “the correct distribution of processes” is the right term here. I suggest removing “correct”.
- Page 18, line 572: Please revise the text since the functional unit is something that you define within your LCA, and not something that is applied to.
- Page 18, line 572: “REMIND SSP1-PkBudg500 was selected as the main model”. Clarify that REMIND is the model and SSP1-PkBudg500 is the scenario.
- Page 18, line 579: “Such an approach aims to define a reference model that quantifies the role of hydrogen irrespective of a scenario”. I don’t see the point of this, since the whole analysis is based on the SSP1-PkBudg500 scenario (plus SSP2 and 5 as sensitivity analysis). I don’t think your analysis study hydrogen irrespective of the scenario (perhaps the allocated SOS yes).
reviewer_comments.reviewer_3:
This article investigates whether current plans to expand hydrogen production are compatible with operating within the Earth’s safe operating space. The work also develops an optimization model to investigate whether an optimized portfolio of hydrogen production technologies could safely operate within the ecological capacity of the planet. The topic is highly relevant and timely. Below I provide some comments that require some attention before proceeding any further:
- Previous works already investigated the planetary boundaries impact of hydrogen production, yet the authors critically assessed them concluding that further refinements were still necessary to draw more meaningful conclusions. However, the final conclusion they present in this work, namely that future hydrogen production is unsustainable, remains somehow very similar. I still see the value of the analysis, but it needs to be more clearly stated in the abstract and conclusions. Moreover, the current study is also affected by a range of methodological choices and uncertainties, some of which were not analyzed with enough depth, as discussed next.
- Different sharing principles should be explored to study the robustness of the results depending on the downscaling approach.
- The calculations are affected by several uncertainty sources, including uncertainties in the background, foreground, characterization factors and absolute thresholds. Please describe all of them in detail and explain how they were accounted for, which remains unclear to me (it seems some were considered and others not, and an exhaustive discussion of this topic is missing).
- The authors use the TCM model to perform the calculations. They mention that a data aggregation step was carried out when building the LP. Please provide more details, as it is very hard to understand how the model works. This aggregation inevitably leads to some information loss, which should be discussed.
- It remains unclear how the premise data is integrated into the LP, and whether the scenario in premise is fully consistent with the IAM scenario for which the calculations were done. Moreover, I wonder why the authors did not explore other scenarios, at least the ones available in premise.
- The authors let the model optimize the amount of DAC required. I wonder if this leads to an inconsistency in the model, as the premise scenario in the background assumes already a given DAC capacity that might differ from the optimal capacity found by the LP model. If so, how would this affect the results?
Overall, this is a nice piece that goes beyond previous studies on a highly relevant topic connected to future energy systems design. The work would benefit from a more exhaustive description of the methods, perhaps complemented by additional calculations to further evaluate the effect of uncertainties. This would enhance the robustness and relevance of the findings.

Comment 9: The implementation of interactions between planetary boundaries is not entirely clear. At page

to carbon dioxide emission to the atmosphere. Thus, a significant change in the LSC control variable would

Thank you for raising this important aspect. In our study, the interaction model serves as an essential guide
for our optimisation model to prioritise the minimisation of impact from influential Earth-system processes. This
17
is important as it could ultimately render the safe operating space smaller than what is currently reported in
several studies12,31. These interactions would account for feedback loops that could have an amplifying or
stabilising influence on other boundaries10,42–45. Beyond life cycle optimisation, the interactions are operational
for any absolute environmental sustainability assessment studies focusing on planetary boundaries.
Given the above, simply adding indirect emissions such as those from land clearing to the inventory of
processes would capture the independent environmental pressure but not the amplifying or stabilising response
due to feedback loops with other Earth-system processes. In addition, such an approach would assume the
independence of land clearing CO2 emissions from all other Earth-system processes beyond climate change. Land
clearing CO2 emissions are only part of the mechanisms captured by the interaction model10,46. The climate
response due to changes in other state control variables would also be quite difficult to capture at a life cycle
inventory stage, and for several reasons. First, to adjust elementary flows to account for interactions – thereby
contributing directly to an impact category – LCA practitioners would need to know in advance the environmental
response of Earth-system processes (feedback loop). Second, there will be an issue of proportionality between
affected Earth system processes, and a normalisation step would be required for all elementary flows involved.
Third, interaction parameters between all elementary flows would have to be defined for known interactions
and for each biophysical system. The ecoinvent database lists more than 4700 elementary flows; attempting to
model the environmental response at an LCI stage would be quite challenging and tedious.
At the impact characterisation stage, to the best of our knowledge, there are no impact characterisation
methods that integrate these feedback loops between Earth-system processes. This is particularly the case for
planetary boundary-based characterisation methods, where environmental pressure is modelled but the
response is not. It is worth noting that significant uncertainty remains for the interaction model due to its
infancy10. However, Earth-system processes are strongly interdependent10,43–46 and assessing them
independently poses a greater risk of overlooking the true planetary footprint of human activities. Hence, until
recent changes43,44 are operational for absolute environmental sustainability assessments, our approach can be
seen as an initial and conservative one.
In summary, the interaction model focuses on the interdependent environmental response rather than the
independent environmental pressure. The impact characterisation captures the environmental pressure, while
the interdependent response is done by the interaction model. We have also clarified that modelling emissions
directly at an LCI stage could be challenging compared to our more straightforward approach. In Revision 9, we
clarify the added value of the interaction model to this extent.

Thank you for your important comment. We agree that in the initial version of the manuscript, some
uncertainties were not comprehensively discussed nor clearly stated. We therefore implemented Revision 16.
We briefly describe how we addressed uncertainties below.
Regarding the uncertainties in the background system, we purposefully excluded this uncertainty as it would
technically create more uncertainty62. Indeed, the traditional approach is to perform random sampling of
coefficients in the LCA database using Montecarlo analysis and assuming their independence. However, these
coefficients are strongly correlated and cannot be sampled randomly without creating large mass and energy
imbalance62. We note a recent paper on the topic from Kim et al.63, but their approach is hardly operational
with our optimisation framework. We therefore excluded background system uncertainties for this reason. For
the characterisation part, we relied on the characterisation factors from Ryberg et al.24 and Bachmann et al.26,
who used biosphere integrity characterisation factors from Galan Martin et al.25. None of these studies has
provided uncertainties for characterisation factors, and we were unable to determine these uncertainties.
We include uncertainties related to the environmental space for global hydrogen production across our AR6-
derived scenario ensemble. More scenarios were included (n=32, instead of n=20 in the initial version) to
increase diversity in IAM models and mitigate bias towards REMIND scenarios. As discussed in comment 23, we
were unable to derive more downscaling principles from this scenario ensemble. This is another source of
uncertainty, which we discuss in Revision 15.
Also, premise scenarios are not part of the AR6 dataset (as pointed out in Comment 26). We therefore had to
validate these against the climate objective we defined (1.9W m-2 forcing by 2100). This aspect is discussed in.
From this validation, we were able to use only 3 scenarios (REMIND SSPx-PkBudg500 scenarios). There is a
significant bias towards REMIND models, which raises some uncertainties in this aspect.
Beyond the above, the interaction model is still in its early stages of development, and several interaction
parameters lack uncertainties. The authors also omitted some interactions due to a lack of data or understanding
of interaction mechanisms10. We were unable to use these uncertainties confidently and therefore excluded
them from our analysis.

Dear editor and reviewers of the manuscript “Pathways to global hydrogen production within
planetary boundaries” with ID: NCOMMS-25-07779A. We appreciate your constructive comments
and thank you for taking the time to review our work.
We confirm that we have addressed each comment in the revised manuscript as outlined in the
sections below. Please find the reviewers’ comments in blue, our response in black, and the changes
made to address the comments in red, with key revisions highlighted in grey. Also, for clarity, we
highlight references to revisions or to line number in blue.
Reviewer 2 - Comment 1 to 8
Comment 1: The authors have made commendable efforts to improve the clarity of the
methodology and findings, and to address reviewers’ comments. The revised version is significantly
clearer and more accessible. However, after reviewing this improved manuscript, I have additional
technical concerns.
Thank you for your interest in our work and for the time invested to review it. We address your
additional concerns below.
Comment 2: At a more fundamental level, I have serious reservations about the suitability of
prospective LCA combined with planetary boundaries to determine whether a product system can
be considered “absolutely” sustainable in the future (in contrast to the more common application to
determine whether product system A performs relatively better than B). An inherent limitation of
prospective LCAs is that the results and conclusions are only valid under the specific conditions
represented by the background and foreground LCIs. Many background processes remain
unchanged even when using premise, meaning that by 2050 they may still reflect current (or in many
cases outdated) practices. This is particularly important given that the authors identify embodied
emissions from the manufacturing of renewable electricity technologies as a key driver of hydrogen’s
unsustainability. In this context, several upstream processes such as heat sources in industrial
processes are often not updated in premise. Similarly, emissions of nitrogen and phosphorus from
copper mining and the management of sulfidic tailings are highly uncertain and remain largely
unchanged. While these assumptions may be acceptable for comparative LCAs of product systems, I
believe they pose significant limitations when applied to absolute sustainability. These assumptions
may be enough for addressing the research question “How do different hydrogen production
pathways perform under a given set of predefined conditions?” Such an analysis provides important
insights into relative performances across alternatives and future hotspots that deserve attention
(e.g., that sulfidic tailings from copper mining need to be managed in a better way). In contrast, I find
it problematic to conclude that a product system is “absolutely” unsustainable by 2025 due to
impacts associated with industrial practices representative of conditions from 25-30 years back. The
authors acknowledge the limitations of potentially unrepresentative LCIs. However, I believe this
raises a more fundamental question about what “absolute unsustainable” truly represents in the
context of prospective LCAs (and how fair it is maybe).
understand your concern as we investigated this aspect and tried to find potential solutions to
mitigate the biogeochemical emissions of renewables. Ultimately, we were unable to address it due
to a lack of data (line 332) – we do not know how these emissions would be tackled in the future of
mining.
As correctly mentioned, premise has inherent limitations regarding the processes that can be
“updated”. When basing the “update” on IAM scenarios, it is only possible to update processes if the
corresponding data is available in scenarios used. Emissions resulting from copper mining or other
activities with relatively low climate change impacts are generally not represented in IAM scenarios.
This explains their omission from the “update”. From this basis, one can easily conclude that this
issue entirely stems from the prospective LCA part of our analysis. Thus, it would naturally be a
limitation in all prospective environmental sustainability assessments, both absolute and relative. If
these limitations are acceptable in pLCA, they should also be acceptable in AESA.
To be more specific, in a relative assessment, when answering the following research question:
“How do different hydrogen production pathways perform under a given set of predefined
conditions?”, the predefined conditions are limited to the scenario data. Non-updated processes
could also shape the conclusions (and fairness). For example, two processes (say, A and B), could rely
on different upstream processes while providing the same function. If some upstream processes of A
are omitted in the premise update, B’s relative environmental performance could be found more eco-
efficient and also shape conclusions. It is thus a problem inherent to IAM-based pLCA, and not
specifically prospective AESA. To the best of our knowledge, it is very difficult (if not impossible) to
update the entire background system data prospectively. This would require knowing the future
technical performance of thousands of processes. Despite these limitations, premise is an accepted
software because it can improve the accuracy of prospective impact scores for given environmental
scenarios, and for studies into the future. The alternative to using prospective approaches like
premise would be to assume that the environmental performance of all technologies will remain at
its current state into the future.
That said, we understand your concern relates to the sharp sustainability conclusion we derive
from our results given this inherent limitation. We therefore implement revision 1 to put emphasis
on the likelihood of sustainability for hydrogen production and that our conclusions are solely based
on our model and known limitations.
Revision 1. Added limitations to sustainability results
At line 21, 72,and 283, where we report our key takeaways, we added “likely unsustainable” to
soften the sharp sustainability statement previously made. We use “likely” to highlight what is
supported by our results while leaving enough room for uncertainties.
However, our results depend on technologies that remain unproven at scale1–3 and do not account
for potential future improvements or breakthroughs in the upstream hydrogen value chain.
At line 347, we added:
However, this is subject to future technological options that may not be accurately represented in
this work.
In addition, from line 417 to 428, we expand the discussion on that particular topic:
Uncertainty also arises from the representation of future technologies in prospective background
systems. The Premise software can only reflect future efficiency improvements for processes present
in future scenarios. It thereby excludes improvement processes that are not represented in these
scenarios and ignores potential technological breakthroughs. For instance, global hydrogen
production could approach sustainability if future processes substantially reduce nitrogen and
phosphorus emissions associated with renewable electricity technologies. Similarly, this assessment
does not account for emerging capillary-feed4 electrolysis designs or advances in abated fossil
pathways, including electrified reformer furnaces5 or improved pre- and post-combustion carbon

Nevertheless, updating background system data using Premise remains a state-of-the-art approach
for improving the accuracy of future life-cycle impacts under a given climate target.
Comment 3: I also have a question about carbon accounting in the case of biogas for biomethane
production followed by reforming to hydrogen coupled with CCS. The authors explain that they do
not account for biogenic carbon. However, biomethane with CCS is potentially a negative emissions
technology. Yet, since the authors used the ecoinvent cut-off system model, the CO2 uptake during
biomass growth is disconnected from the waste management process (i.e., it is accounted for in the
corresponding agricultural activity). How did the authors ensure a correct carbon balance? I believe
this is important since the results suggest that “bio-based production shows the worst planetary 223
footprint – climate change and biosphere integrity transgressed ~229 and 180 times” (line 222).
Thank you for your comment on this important aspect that deserves more clarifications. We
provide the rationale for this important assumption below.
First, as correctly pointed out in the comment, under the cut-off system model, the uptake and
emissions are reported in the original activity. Our process for hydrogen production from
biomethane is based on Antonini et al.6. While the authors expanded their system boundaries to add
the uptake, we refrain from adopting such an approach. For secondary biomass e.g., waste organic
food, sewage sludge, manure, it is more relevant to look at the avoided/created emissions owing to
4
recycling secondary biomass7. This is to avoid the misleading conclusion that secondary biomass
would have had the same impact if not used. It could be true when looking at long time horizons, but
not on an annual basis as imposed by planetary boundaries (Figure.1). In the case of fuel production,
carbon emissions necessarily occur at a much faster rate than the uptake. To sustain such a
production, more biomass need to be used continuously.
Second, for the planetary boundary for climate impacts, peak environmental pressures matter
more in our case than a net carbon balance over 100 years. Unlike traditional LCA that focuses on the
impact created during a product system’s life cycle, in planetary boundaries based LCA, the
assessment is on annual pressure basis. As pointed out by Ryberg et al.8, time integrated impacts
methods are not suitable for the control variables of planetary boundaries. If we apply sufficient
pressure on Earth system processes in a given year, the environmental response may lead to
irreversible changes that cannot be captured by time integrated approaches. For this reason,
planetary boundaries-based characterisation methods rely on continuous annual emission rates
rather than a pulse emission decay over 100 years8,9.
That said if we emit a large amount of biogenic carbon today, until it is recaptured by carbon sinks,
it has the same effect on the Earth system as fossil carbon emissions. Current carbon accounting
approaches based on GWP100, overlook this aspect inherent to planetary boundaries. While we
agree that biogenic carbon accounting is an important aspect, due to the lack of proper accounting
approaches with regards to planetary boundaries and the implications of our results, we believe it is
more conservative not to discount biogenic carbon.
To exemplify this aspect further, we can compare the global temperature response to 1GtC
emitted as a pulse during hydrogen production or spread over a 30-year period in landfill (Figure.1).
Here we chose landfill as it is the most common disposal of waste that will not be recycled in any way.
Landfills provide anaerobic conditions. It could take 5 to 7 years to reach peak emissions and decades
for carbon ultimately going to the atmosphere to be completely released10. The 30-years, evenly
distributed emission period can be seen as conservative. To be more conservative, we can also
assume that all the carbon from landfill is emitted to the air, while in reality, some would end up in
soils. For a fair comparison with hydrogen production, we can reasonably assume that landfills are
properly managed with all methane emissions being flared. As can be seen in Figure.1, at long time
horizons (≥100years), both responses would be similar which confirms current carbon accounting
approaches used in LCA. However, in the short term for nearly 25 years, there is a large positive
difference, more relevant for an assessment on planetary boundaries, that is overlooked when
looking at long time horizons.
This short illustrative example is not perfect and has many flaws, but it clearly shows that current
carbon accounting approaches from traditional life cycle assessment are not directly applicable for
an assessment on planetary boundaries. Also, there is a potential asymmetry between carbon
5
emissions and uptake that deserves further attention11. These aspects require further
methodological work that we consider out of scope.
Figure 1. Comparison of global temperature response to 1GtC from pulse and spread emission profiles. On a
100 years horizon, both approach would lead to the same results. On a yearly basis, current carbon accounting
approaches fail to represent the pressure on Earth system processes. Model was sourced from Ricke and
Caldeira12.
Overall, our assumption to treat biogenic carbon the same as fossil carbon is conservative. Future
work is needed to investigate this aspect more thoroughly. Despite this assumption, our results
remain consistent with most projections from the IRENA13 or IEA14–16. To clarify this aspect more in
detail in the manuscript, we implement Revision 2.

Comment 4: I find the use of IAM scenario outputs in the revised version somewhat confusing. The
authors state that they align with recommendations from a recently published Bortoli et al paper by
using an ensemble of 32 IAM scenarios to define future global hydrogen production volumes and the
corresponding allocated SOS. However, for the prospective LCA modelling, they rely on 3 IAM
scenarios provided within premise. This is acknowledged at line 495. Although both sets of scenarios
are consistent in terms of their climate targets (i.e., achieving a radiative forcing of 1.9–2.25 W/m²),
this approach introduces a substantial inconsistency in terms of hydrogen demand and sectoral
structure. For example, I believe the electricity mix in each IAM scenario is influenced by the level of
hydrogen demand assumed in that scenario. Therefore, using the range of hydrogen demand from
the 32-scenario ensemble may not be representative of the sectoral dynamics embedded in the 3
premise scenarios.
Thank you for your comment on this interesting point. We understand the concern, however, as
previously said, we do not assess the embedded sectoral dynamics of each scenario. If a scenario
meets our climate target, this implies that it has an underlying sectoral configuration that enables it.
The heterogeneity of sectoral configurations is also not a substantial inconsistency, quite the
opposite, it provides robustness to our outcomes. The point for comparison across scenarios is not
“how similar should be their sectoral configurations”, but rather what trends appear across scenarios
when they are built to meet the climate target. These trends include hydrogen production volumes,
electrical mix configurations, and in the case of premise, expected prospective impact scores.
To be more specific, all 32 scenarios in our AR6-based ensemble have different sectoral
configurations, with different electrical mixes and different hydrogen production volumes. The
common point between all these scenarios is their sectoral configurations aligned for the fulfillment
of the climate target. The approach is similar to that of the IPCC AR618,19 where scenarios are classified
by categories – e.g., C1 for scenarios limiting global warming to 1.5°C, C2 for 2°C. From each category,
a need for hydrogen, electricity generation sources or carbon management technologies be
established quantitatively – a good example for hydrogen is shown in figure Fig. 4b in Johnson et al.3.
Similarly, when using Premise, prospective and quantitative impact scores are derived from
underlying sectoral configurations designed to meet the climate target. Ideally, the entire
7
assessment would be based on a single scenario ensemble. However, technical limitations (i.e.,
dimension mismatch) restricted the Premise ensemble to the REMIND PkBudg500 scenarios (n=3).
Despite the small premise sample size, Supplementary Fig. 17 shows that the uncertainty range of
the Premise ensemble adequately covers that of the broader AR6 ensemble by 2100. Therefore,
sampling impact scores from this range in our Monte Carlo analysis should sufficiently represent the
scores derived from the AR6 ensemble.
In summary, even if hydrogen production volumes and sectoral dynamics from the Premise
ensemble is different from the AR6 ensemble, our uncertainty range ensures the consistency of
impacts scores with the climate targets.

reviewer_comments.reviewer_2:
The authors have made commendable efforts to improve the clarity of the methodology and findings, and to address reviewers’ comments. The revised version is significantly clearer and more accessible. However, after reviewing this improved manuscript, I have additional technical concerns.
1. At a more fundamental level, I have serious reservations about the suitability of prospective LCA combined with planetary boundaries to determine whether a product system can be considered “absolutely” sustainable in the future (in contrast to the more common application to determine whether product system A performs relatively better than B). An inherent limitation of prospective LCAs is that the results and conclusions are only valid under the specific conditions represented by the background and foreground LCIs. Many background processes remain unchanged even when using premise, meaning that by 2050 they may still reflect current (or in many cases outdated) practices. This is particularly important given that the authors identify embodied emissions from the manufacturing of renewable electricity technologies as a key driver of hydrogen’s unsustainability. In this context, several upstream processes such as heat sources in industrial processes are often not updated in premise. Similarly, emissions of nitrogen and phosphorus from copper mining and the management of sulfidic tailings are highly uncertain and remain largely unchanged. While these assumptions may be acceptable for comparative LCAs of product systems, I believe they pose significant limitations when applied to absolute sustainability. These assumptions may be enough for addressing the research question “How do different hydrogen production pathways perform under a given set of predefined conditions?” Such an analysis provides important insights into relative performances across alternatives and future hotspots that deserve attention (e.g., that sulfidic tailings from copper mining need to be managed in a better way). In contrast, I find it problematic to conclude that a product system is “absolutely” unsustainable by 2025 due to impacts associated with industrial practices representative of conditions from 25-30 years back. The authors acknowledge the limitations of potentially unrepresentative LCIs. However, I believe this raises a more fundamental question about what “absolute unsustainable” truly represents in the context of prospective LCAs (and how fair it is maybe).
2. I also have a question about carbon accounting in the case of biogas for biomethane production followed by reforming to hydrogen coupled with CCS. The authors explain that they do not account for biogenic carbon. However, biomethane with CCS is potentially a negative emissions technology. Yet, since the authors used the ecoinvent cut-off system model, the CO2 uptake during biomass growth is disconnected from the waste management process (i.e., it is accounted for in the corresponding agricultural activity). How did the authors ensure a correct carbon balance? I believe this is important since the results suggest that “bio-based production shows the worst planetary 223 footprint – climate change and biosphere integrity transgressed ~229 and 180 times” (line 222).
3. I find the use of IAM scenario outputs in the revised version somewhat confusing. The authors state that they align with recommendations from a recently published Bortoli et al paper by using an ensemble of 32 IAM scenarios to define future global hydrogen production volumes and the corresponding allocated SOS. However, for the prospective LCA modelling, they rely on 3 IAM scenarios provided within premise. This is acknowledged at line 495. Although both sets of scenarios are consistent in terms of their climate targets (i.e., achieving a radiative forcing of 1.9–2.25 W/m²), this approach introduces a substantial inconsistency in terms of hydrogen demand and sectoral structure. For example, I believe the electricity mix in each IAM scenario is influenced by the level of hydrogen demand assumed in that scenario. Therefore, using the range of hydrogen demand from the 32-scenario ensemble may not be representative of the sectoral dynamics embedded in the 3 premise scenarios.
4. The results indicate that the optimal hydrogen mix for 2025 requires approximately 49% to come from electrolysis. However, it is well known that as of 2024, green hydrogen produced via electrolysis accounts for about 1%. It would be helpful if the authors clarified in the manuscript that these figures represent a hypothetical snapshot of what would be needed today to remain within the allocated SOS. Moreover, this raises questions about whether the authors should have calibrated their model against empirical data to ensure consistency between modelled projections and current realities.
Other minor comments:
1. Line 432: the authors indicate that their “system-based approach can also be interpreted as consequential to some extent”. This consequential approach does not seem to align with current recommendations for “absolute sustainability assessment”, where it is stated that “An important requirement, no matter the scale of the activity studied, is that the accounting approach follows the attributional accounting philosophy”
(https://publications.jrc.ec.europa.eu/repository/handle/JRC142099). The idea of a consequential approach is also repeated at line 315.
2. Line 433: “the functional unit as the “global annual hydrogen production with a carbon capture option”. This is not very clear, as the optimal annual hydrogen production include several pathways such as electrolytic hydrogen. Could the authors be more precise about the meaning of “with a carbon capture option”?
3. Line 336: “Our results confirm that abated fossil production has an environmental performance comparable to electrolysis and can serve as a bridging pathway”… which however is entirely dependent on the conditions assumed in the background system for the raw materials supply and manufacturing of renewable technologies.
reviewer_comments.reviewer_3: The authors successfully addressed my previous comments, so the manuscript is now ready for publication.
